summary: Slovenia is an EU and Schengen member: EU/EEA citizens enter freely with an ID card, around 60 visa-waiver nationalities — including the US, UK, Japan and most of the Americas — get 90 days in any 180 across the whole Schengen Area, and other travelers need a Schengen visa.

defaultStayWindow.text: 90 days in any rolling 180-day period, counted across the whole Schengen Area rather than per country. The day you arrive counts as the first day and the day you leave counts as the last. Leaving and coming back does not reset the allowance: on any given day, days already spent anywhere in the area during the preceding 180 still count against the 90.

roadVignette.text: Slovenian motorways and expressways run on an e-vignette linked to the number plate; vehicles without one may not enter a toll road. Two stretches sit outside it: the Karavanke tunnel to Austria, which costs €9 per crossing for a car at the Hrušica toll booth, and — since January 1, 2026 — the coastal H5 and H6 expressways, which no longer need a vignette at all.

tips.text: The UK government's travel advice says you must buy an e-vignette to drive on Slovenian motorways. Weekly, monthly and yearly e-vignettes are sold at petrol stations, post offices and DARS offices, and online only on the official DARS website (evinjeta.dars.si).

The UK government's travel advice tells hikers to plan for the weakest member of the group, use a map with marked paths, check whether mountain huts are open and keep off closed trails, and notes that bears live in wooded areas throughout Slovenia. For mountain rescue, call 112.
The EU says visa-exempt travellers will need an ETIAS travel authorisation once the system starts. ETIAS is not yet in operation, and the EU will announce the start date several months before launch.

faq.question: Do I need a visa for Slovenia?
faq.answer: EU citizens enter freely with a passport or ID card. Citizens of around 60 visa-waiver countries — including the US, UK, Canada, Australia, Japan and most of the Americas — get 90 days in any 180-day period across the Schengen Area. Everyone else needs a Schengen visa from a Slovenian embassy or visa center.

faq.question: Is Slovenia in the Schengen Area?
faq.answer: Yes. Your 90/180-day visa-free allowance is shared across the whole Schengen Area. Canada's travel advice notes that Schengen countries may temporarily reintroduce controls at internal borders, so you may have to pass through immigration controls when entering Slovenia even from another Schengen country.

faq.question: Will I need ETIAS for Slovenia?
faq.answer: ETIAS is not yet in operation. Once it starts, visa-exempt travellers will need the authorisation before their trip. The EU says applying costs EUR 20 (some travellers are exempt), and an authorisation is valid for up to three years or until the passport expires, for short stays in 30 European countries.

faq.question: What currency does Slovenia use?
faq.answer: The euro, according to Canada's travel advice. No official source we could read describes how widely cards are accepted; Canada's advice says ATMs are rare in mountain regions and small villages.

faq.question: Can I day-trip from Slovenia to Croatia or Italy?
faq.answer: Yes. Italy and Croatia are both in the Schengen Area, so you need no separate visa. Schengen countries may temporarily reintroduce border controls, and the EU says you must then show a valid passport or ID card. Days anywhere in the Schengen Area count toward the same 90/180 allowance.
